title: Some people think the lesson of the talents is about ability.
paragraphs: Some people think the lesson of the talents is about ability.
It isn’t.
It is about what we do with what God places in our hands.
In Matthew 25, Jesus tells a story about a master who entrusted his servants with resources before leaving on a journey.

One received five talents.
Another received two.
Another received one.
Right away we notice something important.
The master did not give everyone the same amount.
And that alone answers one of the biggest questions people wrestle with today.

Why do some people seem to have more opportunities?
More influence?
More gifts?
Because the kingdom of God has never been built on equal assignments.
It has always been built on faithful stewardship.
The servant with five talents went and invested them.
The servant with two talents did the same.
Both doubled what they were given.
But the servant with one talent did something very different.
He buried it.
He hid it in the ground.
Not because he hated his master.
Not because he wanted to rebel.
But because he was afraid.
And that is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because many people today are not living in rebellion against God.
They are living in burial.
They buried the gift.
They buried the calling.
They buried the opportunity.
They buried the obedience God asked for.
Not because they lacked ability…
But because fear convinced them not to move.
Fear whispers things like:

“What if you fail?”
“What if you are not good enough?”
“What if someone judges you?”
“What if you lose what little you have?”
And slowly, quietly, a person begins to hide the very thing God entrusted to them.
But the most striking part of this parable happens when the master returns.
He does not ask the servants why they didn’t receive the same amount.
He does not compare the one with two to the one with five.
He asks something much deeper.
“What did you do with what I gave you?”
That question removes every excuse we tend to lean on.
Because God will never ask you why you were not someone else.
He will never ask why your platform was smaller.
He will never ask why your opportunities looked different.
But He will ask what you did with what was already placed in your hands.
And this is where the beauty of the story appears.
The servant with five talents hears the words:
“Well done, good and faithful servant.”
The servant with two talents hears the exact same words.
Not a reduced version.
Not a smaller approval.
The same reward.
Why?
Because in the kingdom of God, faithfulness is the real measurement.
Not comparison.
Not visibility.
Not applause.
Faithfulness.
And that truth is freeing.
You do not need someone else’s assignment to please God.
You only need to be faithful with yours.
But the third servant reveals a warning we cannot ignore.
He says to the master:
“I was afraid.”
Those three words expose something powerful.
Fear can become the graveyard of calling.
Fear can bury potential.
Fear can silence obedience.
Fear can delay purpose until years pass by.
Some gifts are not destroyed by sin.
They are destroyed by neglect.
Some callings are not lost in rebellion.
They are lost in hesitation.
Some destinies are not stolen by the enemy.
They are quietly buried by fear.
And the tragedy is this:
A buried talent still belongs to the master.
It was never meant to stay in the ground.
It was meant to be used.
To grow.
To multiply.
To bless others.
To glorify God.
The servant thought burying it was the safest option.
But in reality, it was the most dangerous choice he could make.
Because the master expected movement.
Stewardship.
Responsibility.
And the truth is, every one of us has something God has entrusted to us.
Maybe it is your voice.
Maybe it is your influence.
Maybe it is wisdom.
Maybe it is creativity.
Maybe it is leadership.
Maybe it is compassion.
Maybe it is the courage to speak truth.
It may not look like five talents.
It may feel like two.
It may even feel like one.
But if God placed it in your hands, it is not small.
It is sacred.
And heaven notices what we do with it.
So the real question of this parable is not:
“Who received more?”
The real question is:
What are you doing with what God gave you?
Are you investing it?
Using it?
Serving others with it?
Growing it?
Or have you buried something that was meant to live?
Because one day, every servant in the story faced the same moment.
The master returned.
And every life eventually reaches that moment.
Not when we compare gifts.
But when we give an account.
The lesson I learned from this parable is simple, but weighty:
God does not expect you to manage someone else’s calling.
But He does expect you to be faithful with yours.
So do not bury what God entrusted to you.
Do not hide what heaven intended to multiply.
Do not let fear become the grave where your calling is forgotten.
Because one day the Master will ask the same question He asked in the story:
“What did you do with what I gave you?”
And the most beautiful words a servant can ever hear are still the same today:
“Well done, good and faithful servant.”
Matthew 25:14–30
Engagement Question (important for algorithm reach):
What is one gift, opportunity, or calling God placed in your hands that you know you should stop burying?
